Photograph: Alex Bowie/Getty Images Movies John Irvin, British film-maker who directed Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy, dies aged 86 The director’s BBC hit opened the door to Hollywood action films including Hamburger Hill, The Dogs of War and Raw Deal Sian Cain Wed 19 Aug 2026 00.31 EDT Last modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 00.33 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google John Irvin, the British film-maker who directed the Bafta-winning BBC miniseries Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy , as well as films including Hamburger Hill, The Dogs of War and Raw Deal, has died aged 86. Irvin died “peacefully at home” on 11 August, surrounded by his family, his producer Claire Evans confirmed to the Guardian. Over a 50-year career that spanned TV, documentaries and action films, Irvin was known for his versatility, working with everyone from Fred Astaire to Arnold Schwarzenegger. His most famous work was Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy, the John le Carré adaptation starring Alec Guinness as the spy George Smiley; Guinness once wrote of his admiration of Irvin, “a director with balls behind the camera!” Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy: 40 years on, the labyrinthine thriller is still TV caviar Read more Born in 1940 in Wallasey, Cheshire, Irvin started out as a student at the London Film School and worked at British Movietone News. In 1963 he released his first film, the documentary Gala Day, and a documentary short, Inheritance, which was narrated by Richard Burton and won Irvin his first Bafta. After he documented the North Yemen war, Irvin said MI6 took an interest in his work but he was never formally enlisted as a spy. “I was far too left wing, for a start, but was anti-apartheid, anti-war, anti-nuclear. They were probably well aware of my leftwing activities, so I was certainly not involved in any hanky-panky,” he said in a 2021 interview. Irvin directed several short films for the BBC and ITV, including 1969’s The Peasants Revolt, starring Anthony Hopkins in his first TV role. In the 1970s he moved into TV drama, directing The Nearly Man, Hard Times starring Timothy West, and Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy with Guinness, Ian Richardson, Patrick Stewart and Beryl Reid. The miniseries won two Baftas from six nominations and was nominated for an Emmy for outstanding limited series. View image in fullscreen Alec Guinness and Siân Phillips during filming of the 1979 miniseries Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy The success of Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy opened the door to Hollywood, with Irvin directing The Dogs of War (1980) starring Christopher Walken and Tom Berenger; the horror film Ghost Story (1981) starring Fred Astaire; Champions (1984) starring John Hurt; Turtle Diary (1985) starring Ben Kingsley, Glenda Jackson and Michael Gambon; Raw Deal (1986) starring Schwarzenegger; Hamburger Hill (1987) starring Don Cheadle and Dylan McDermott; and Next of Kin (1989) starring Patrick Swayze and Liam Neeson. ‘The aim was to give Kevin Costner’s version a good kicking’: director John Irvin on his anti-Thatcher Robin Hood Read more In 1991 Irvin directed Robin Hood with Patrick Bergin and a 20-year-old Uma Thurman; the film was deliberately commissioned as a rival to Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves starring Kevin Costner. While Irvin’s film was released two months before Costner’s, the latter was a megahit at the box office. “It was very much a stand-alone film with the aim of giving Kevin Costner’s version a good kicking if we could,” Irvin told the Guardian in May . “The studio wanted to go immediately because they wanted to pre-empt the Costner … I didn’t get involved in that mess, I just put my head down. Politics were left to the producers and executives.” In the 2000s, Irvin focused on independent cinema, directing films such as Shiner (2000) with Michael Caine, The Moon And The Stars (2006) with Alfred Molina and Jonathan Pryce, and The Garden Of Eden (2008) with Jack Huston, Mena Suvari and Richard E Grant. Irvin’s final film was 2016’s Mandela’s Gun , a biopic of Nelson Mandela focused on his experience as a guerrilla fighter for the African National Congress. Irvin was working on a new cut of the film at the time of his death. Irvin is survived by his three children, Emilie, Luke and Amy, and two grandchildren. Photograph: Kin Cheung/AP UK news Two arrested in London on suspicion of aiding Iran’s foreign intelligence Arrests of woman, 42, and man, 60, follow Met search of addresses in north and north-west London Press Association Thu 10 Sep 2026 09.54 EDT Last modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 10.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A man and a woman have been arrested by counter-terrorism police in London on suspicion of assisting Iran’s foreign intelligence service. The arrests of the 42-year-old woman and 60-year-old man were made after searches at addresses in north and north-west London on 24 June, the Metropolitan police said. A third property was also searched in north-west London on 9 September after their arrest under the National Security Act (NSA). The investigation is not linked to attacks at buildings and venues linked to Jewish and Iranian communities in London, the force added. It is also not thought to be linked to any activity or events linked to the Jewish high holy days period. The man and woman have been released on conditional bail until a date in October. Commander Helen Flanagan, the head of counter-terrorism policing London, said: “We know that news of these arrests will come as a concern to some members of the public, but I want to stress that we do not believe there to be any imminent threat to the wider public in connection with this matter. “We’ve seen a marked increase in the tempo of our work linked to national security and state threats over the past year and this investigation is a continuation of that. “As we’ve shown here, if we suspect any activity could threaten the safety of the UK or the public, then we will not hesitate to take action. “I would also like to remind the public that the overall terrorism threat level is at severe, so we continue to ask for everyone’s support through being vigilant, and if you see or hear anything that doesn’t look right, then please, trust your instincts, and report it to us.” Explore more on these topics UK news news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

They were members of a Toowoomba religious sect known as the Saints. Photograph: BBC View image in fullscreen Elizabeth Struhs died from diabetic ketoacidosis in 2022 after her parents withdrew her insulin. They were members of a Toowoomba religious sect known as the Saints. Photograph: BBC Queensland Child safety staff determined to send Elizabeth Struhs home with parents despite doctors’ concerns, inquest hears Queensland coronial inquest into death of eight-year-old girl continues after 14 members of religious sect were convicted of her manslaughter Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Andrew Messenger Tue 13 Oct 2026 04.53 EDT Last modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 05.17 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google It was impossible to change the mind of child safety staff after they had decided to send Elizabeth Struhs home with her parents despite some of her doctors’ concerns, a police officer has told a coronial inquest into the young girl’s death. Child safety staff decided in 2019 that it would be “more detrimental” to not return Elizabeth, aged six at the time, to her Toowoomba home upon her discharge from hospital after suffering a coma due to diabetic ketoacidosis, a Queensland coroner heard. Elizabeth died at home on 7 January 2022 after her parents withdrew the insulin she needed to survive type 1 diabetes. Her parents were members of a religious sect known as the Saints. The sect did not believe in medicine, and believed Elizabeth would be miraculously healed of her illness or raised from the dead, the inquest heard. All 14 adult members of the sect were convicted of Elizabeth’s manslaughter last year, including her father, Jason Struhs, and mother, Kerrie Struhs. 5:49 Fourteen members of religious sect found guilty of killing eight-year-old Elizabeth Struhs - video The coroner, Ainslie Kirkegaard, heard evidence on Monday from senior doctors at the Queensland children’s hospital who had repeatedly raised the alarm after Elizabeth was hospitalised in a 2019 incident. Kerrie Struhs told the authorities at the time that she didn’t believe in medicine, and had discouraged Elizabeth’s father from seeking medical assistance and to instead trust in prayer, the coroner heard. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Both parents were convicted of not providing the necessaries of life to Elizabeth as a result of the incident, and Kerrie was jailed. After Elizabeth was admitted to hospital in 2019, doctors warned that Kerrie might “sabotage” her long-term treatment for the incurable illness, which requires multiple insulin injections a day, if they lived together, the coroner heard. But the court heard that child safety officers determined she should be returned home to the care of Jason. The coroner heard evidence about a meeting held by the suspected child abuse and neglect team in which the decision was made. It was led by child safety officers, but involved specialist police and health staff. Jason was deemed to be able to provide treatment for Elizabeth, such as insulin injections, the court heard. According to minutes from the meeting, a child safety officer said: “The Queensland children’s hospital is not agreeing with our assessment and have been very vocal about it. I feel that removing her would be more detrimental and we currently have the father stepping up.” On Tuesday, the court heard from a police officer who had attended the meeting. He told the court he’d served as a child safety liaison for 10 years. “I learned early on … you couldn’t change child safety’s mind once they had made their decision,” the officer told the court. “I was never going to change their mind regardless of what I said.” The officer said the attitude was not confined to a single child safety officer. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “It was across the board … they had their own structured decision making tools that they used and we had to respect their decision.” The officer described the approach as “professional courtesy”. Jason was initially willing to provide insulin to Elizabeth – against the wishes of his wife and their other children – but ceased doing so in 2021 after converting to his wife’s religious beliefs and joining her church group, leading to the child’s death. A paediatrician specialist in child safety based at the Toowoomba hospital told the inquest on Tuesday that she was “generally happy” with the way child safety approached the case, including returning Elizabeth home. According to notes taken at a meeting at the time and presented in court, the specialist said Elizabeth would be safe “as long as they are engaging with the hospital and diabetes educator”. “If they stop showing up or engaging then it is likely we would put in a report as we would need to try and find out why.” On Monday, two other doctors at the Queensland children’s hospital in Brisbane told the inquest that they were unhappy with the approach, which one labelled “entirely inadequate to address the risk”. One told the coroner that there had been longstanding poor relations between the Brisbane and Toowoomba hospitals, and their advice was ignored. But the Toowoomba doctor denied the hospitals had a poor relationship. No witnesses appearing at the inquest can be identified for legal reasons. The inquest continues. World News Trump Says He Will ‘Certainly Look at’ Establishing a US Base in Lithuania Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius has said his country would ‘definitely’ be in favor of a permanent U.S. military presence. Save Mark Us Preferred on Google Print U.S. Army soldiers participate in the Saber Strike 26 NATO exercise near Bemowo Piskie, Poland, on May 7, 2026. The exercise involved thousands of troops across Poland and Lithuania, highlighting the U.S. military presence on NATO's eastern flank. Sean Gallup/Getty Images Victoria Friedman 10/6/2026 | Updated: 10/6/2026 0:00 X 1 President Donald Trump has said that he will consider establishing an American military base in Lithuania, with the Baltic country’s prime minister saying Vilnius would be prepared to pay the cost of setting it up. Asked during a press briefing on Oct. 5 if he would consider the move, Trump said, “We’ll certainly look at it.” “Lithuania … I know so many people in that country,” Trump said. “They’re great people.” Last week, Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius told Bloomberg that his country would “definitely” be in favor of a permanent U.S. military base. He said he discussed the proposal during a meeting last month with Trump’s ​envoy John ​Coale, who was in Vilnius helping to facilitate the release of prisoners from Belarus. “We would like to actually have the American troops … with a permanent stationing,” Sinkevicius said on Sept. 29. “We are ready to pay the bill, if that’s the case.” Related Stories Trump Plans Call With Putin to Discuss Possible Pneumonic Plague Case Iceland Occupies Critical Strategic Position for Collective Security, Rubio Says Lithuania is a member of NATO and borders Russia and Moscow’s close ally, Belarus. The United States has ​kept an armored battalion of almost ​1,000 troops in the Baltic nation since 2019 in overlapping rotations, meaning ‌the ⁠troops arrive and leave every few months. Sinkevicius reiterated his support on Oct. 6 for a permanent stationing of U.S. troops, writing in a Facebook post that he was “glad this idea is being taken seriously. Appreciating the contributions of allies to our security.” “The partners only need to make a political decision on permanent deployment of soldiers and Lithuania is ready to cover the related financial costs,” he said. In a follow-up post, Sinkevicius said he had “instructed the Department of Homeland Defense to do their ‘housework’ and present the options and conditions to accommodate permanently deployed U.S. troops.” US Army Base in Poland The calls by Lithuania to have a permanent U.S. base follow Trump last month saying that significant steps had been taken toward setting up a U.S. Army base in Poland, also a NATO country. Trump said it would be a “historic step” for the two nations. The U.S. Army Garrison Poland currently has a presence, but not a permanent base. “GREAT NEWS! Thanks to the bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki, President of Poland, major progress is being made toward establishing a U.S. Army base in Poland,” he wrote on Truth Social on Sept. 17. “If this happens, the location will be announced very soon.” In response to Trump’s announcement, Nawrocki thanked him for his strong commitment to the U.S.-Poland partnership. “We are ready to continue our efforts to strengthen our defense cooperation: seriously, responsibly, and always together,” he said on X at the time. “I can assure you that the Polish government will do its utmost to provide the best possible location for the US Army base.” In August, Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski said Warsaw was holding discussions with Pentagon officials about establishing several U.S. military bases in the country. About 10,000 U.S. troops are stationed in Poland. Timothy Frudd and Reuters contributed to this report. Photograph: AP View image in fullscreen HRW said arrests had been made based on information found on phones, third-party allegations or raids on private premises, while lawyers fear representing those detained. Photograph: AP Global development LGBTQ+ people go into hiding in Senegal as hundreds are arrested At least 320 people detained for ‘acts against nature’ after law criminalising homosexuality toughened, HRW reports Supported by About this content Sarah Johnson Thu 15 Oct 2026 04.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 04.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a new report . More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, according to HIV Justice Network , an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report. Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status. The intensifying crackdown comes as the law criminalising homosexuality in the country was toughened earlier this year. On 11 March, Senegal’s parliament amended the penal code, doubling the maximum prison term for consensual same-sex relations to 10 years. The new law introduced penalties of up to seven years in prison and a fine of 500,000 to 5m CFA francs (£650–£6,500) for promoting homosexuality, or supporting or financing LGBTQ+ people and organisations. Larissa Kojoué, LGBTQ+ rights researcher at Human Rights Watch, said: “LGBTQ+ people are being forced to curb their normal activities … for fear of arrest and increased stigma. Senegal’s government should call a halt to this crackdown, which threatens everyone’s rights.” Same-sex sexual activity was criminalised in Senegal in 1965, but hostility towards LGBTQ+ individuals has grown in recent years. During the 2024 presidential campaign, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, who ended up winning the election, and the former prime minister Ousmane Sonko promised to strengthen laws criminalising same-sex relations , framing the issue as a national priority. Arrests of men and women have happened all over the country. The police say they have arrested people based on information extracted from seized phones , third-party allegations or raids on private premises. The changes to the penal code have had a chilling effect on lawyers, who said they were afraid to represent people for fear of being prosecuted themselves, according to the report. Doctors told Human Rights Watch that the changes were discouraging people from seeking HIV testing and treatment. While there was a 49% fall in new HIV infections in western and central Africa from 2010 to 2022, sub-Saharan Africa remains disproportionately affected by the virus, with 64% of all people living with HIV globally. View image in fullscreen Protesters call for a crackdown on LGBTQ+ people in February in Senegal’s capital, Dakar. The issue was promoted as a national priority in elections. Photograph: Zohra Bensemra/Reuters Sylvie Beaumont, a consultant with HIV Justice Network, said she had received anecdotal evidence that HIV clinics had seen a drop in attendance. “Obviously this is not good for the HIV response because people are going without treatment, they’re not going to get tested,” she said. “The consequences are really bad and it’s sad because Senegal was a country that was doing well with their HIV response. They are shooting themselves in the foot.” She said while the law criminalising deliberate HIV transmission was not part of the reforms to the penal code this year, there had been an “unprecedented” rate of arrests in recent months. She labelled the charges “nonsensical” because it was reported that most people had either only discovered their status upon arrest; were arrested with condoms; or were on treatment that renders transmission of the virus impossible. The report said police had breached confidentiality of ongoing criminal investigations involving suspected LGBTQ+ people by leaking details to the media, which reported personal and confidential information, including HIV status – exposing individuals to social stigma, family rejection, threats and violence. LGBTQ+ people interviewed by Human Rights Watch said the crackdown was instilling fear among their community, and causing them to feel anxious and depressed. Many have gone into hiding, restricted their movements or relocated; some have left the country. The report pointed out that the crackdown flew in the face of domestic and international laws that guaranteed the right to a fair trial, privacy and non-discrimination. The changes to Senegal’s penal code is part of a trend across sub-Saharan Africa towards more punitive legislation directed against LGBTQ+ people. There have been dozens of arrests in Niger since it criminalised “ sexual relations with a person of the same sex ” in February. It was the first time in the country’s history that homosexuality had been criminalised, and followed the introduction of similar laws and penal codes in neighbouring Mali and Burkina Faso within the past two years. All three are ruled by military juntas. In May, Ghana, which already outlaws gay sex, passed legislation criminalising LGBTQ+ “activities” . The bill, which has not been signed into law by the president, is the latest iteration of legislation first proposed in 2021 . In 2023, Uganda’s Anti-Homosexuality Act made homosexual acts punishable by death. http://www.bgnes.com/politics/eu-summit-.text: EU leaders have postponed key decisions on the bloc’s long-term budget and Ukraine’s financial needs until meetings in November and December, following two days of tense talks in Brussels, Politico reports. Against the backdrop of upcoming elections in Spain and France, the European Council summit made no substantial progress. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who arrived in Belgium, received political support but no financial commitments. At a press conference, Zelenskyy urged his European counterparts to draw up a financial plan and warned of the risk of an unprecedented migration crisis, with “20 million Ukrainians” potentially heading towards Europe. “The war next year will cost €155 billion. We need at least €70 billion more from you - for defence, weapons and our resilience,” he said. According to diplomats cited by the publication, European capitals will continue to explore various options, including a new EU loan. The debate over the possible use of around €300 billion in frozen Russian assets to support Ukraine was one of the main topics. Nearly a year after the idea was rejected due to objections from Belgium, France and Italy, several countries called for it to be reconsidered, while EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the frozen assets would be back on the table. “Nothing has changed,” Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said afterwards. “In the short term, the money to support Ukraine must come from sources other than frozen assets.” According to diplomats, the European Commission and national governments are working on alternatives, including funding from allies outside the EU, the mobilisation of funds that have yet to be used, and a new joint loan in addition to the €90 billion loan agreed last year. European Council President António Costa said leaders had agreed that Ukraine’s additional financial needs for 2027 should be covered and had asked the Commission to present a concrete proposal. However, none of the options under discussion received backing at the press conferences held at the end of the summit. The meeting was also presented as an opportunity to break the deadlock in negotiations over the EU’s long-term budget, worth nearly €2 trillion. French President Emmanuel Macron, who will leave office next year ahead of the presidential elections in April and June, warned that he would lack the political mandate to sign an agreement if one was not reached by the end of this year. Despite hours of talks, neither the ‘frugal’ camp, led by Germany, nor the ‘Friends of Cohesion’ group, which is pushing for a larger budget, made any substantial move towards reconciling their positions. “I think a deal is possible by the end of the year,” Macron said, adding that failing to reach an agreement this year would not be “a good approach from a democratic point of view”. On climate and migration, leaders sought to gain tactical advantages. An attempt by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk to soften the ETS2 emissions trading scheme held up discussions for hours on Thursday, but was ultimately rejected. On migration, Denmark, Italy and Poland proposed changes to the conclusions that would explicitly link irregular migration to crime rates and describe it as a threat to the unity of European societies. The proposal received support from around 10 countries, including Hungary, and was indirectly aimed at Spain. There, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s decision to legalise the status of around one million irregular migrants sparked disputes with Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen confirmed that the Commission would present an emergency response framework before the end of the year. It would enable EU countries to respond to sudden, large-scale migration flows, such as those that caused chaos in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta over the summer. However, Meloni and Frederiksen’s efforts failed, as the wording they had proposed was removed from the final conclusions. Macron described the migration debates as excessively politicised, calling them “a major source of division around the table”. | BGNES
